title: 3D Shapes for Grade 2: Faces, Edges & Vertices (with a Free Quiz)
meta_title: 3D Shapes Grade 2: Faces, Edges & Vertices + Quiz
meta_desc: Grade 2 guide to 3D shapes and their faces, edges and vertices - cube, cuboid, sphere, cone, cylinder - plus which solids roll, slide or stack. Free quiz.
excerpt: A dice, a ball and an ice-cream cone teach more about 3D shapes than any diagram. Here is how I help Grade 2 count faces, edges and vertices - and spot solids everywhere - with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 2 child a dice and ask how many flat sides it has, and you will usually get the right answer only after they turn it over and over in their hands. That turning is the whole lesson. The faces, edges and vertices of 3D shapes in Grade 2 are not something to memorise off a page — they are something to touch, roll and count. A dice is a cube, a tin of biscuits is a cylinder, and the ice-cream cone from the corner shop is, well, a cone. Start there, and the vocabulary sticks.

In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, the mistake is jumping straight to the words. A child who can chant ‘six faces, twelve edges, eight vertices’ but cannot point to a single edge on a real box has learned nothing useful. So we count on real objects first, and the words come after.

What faces, edges and vertices actually mean

Three small words carry this whole topic, so let us pin them down with a box in hand:

  • Face — a flat or curved surface you could paint. The top of a matchbox is one face.
  • Edge — the line where two faces meet. Run a finger along the side of a book and you are tracing an edge.
  • Vertex — a corner point where edges meet. The pointy tip of a party hat is a vertex. The plural is vertices, and yes, that word trips up adults too.

Here is a caveat worth saying out loud: a sphere and a cylinder have curved surfaces, and a ball has no corners or edges at all. Children often want every solid to have neat corners like a cube. It does not, and that is fine.

Faces, edges and vertices of the five Grade 2 solids

These are the five solids the NCERT-aligned Grade 2 syllabus expects children to recognise. I would not add more at this age — five, learned properly, beats ten learned as a blur.

SolidFacesEdgesVerticesEveryday example
Cube6 (all flat, square)128Dice, sugar cube
Cuboid6 (all flat)128Matchbox, brick
Sphere1 (curved)00Ball, orange
Cone2 (1 flat, 1 curved)11Ice-cream cone, party hat
Cylinder3 (2 flat, 1 curved)20Tin, candle, pipe

Notice the cube and cuboid share the same numbers. That is the counter-intuitive bit children enjoy: a matchbox and a dice are cousins, both with 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices — the cube just happens to have every face the same square size.

Flat faces and curved surfaces

The quickest way to sort solids is to ask one question: does it have any flat faces, or is it all curved? A ball is pure curve. A tin has two flat circles on the ends and a curved wrap around the middle. A cone has one flat circle at the bottom and a curved surface that sweeps up to a point.

The paint test

I ask children to imagine painting one face a different colour, then rolling the shape. On a cube every side is a fresh flat face to paint. On a sphere there is nothing to divide up — it is one endless curved surface. This little game does more for understanding than any worksheet definition.

Which solids roll, slide and stack?

This is the part every child loves, because you actually test it. Put the shapes on a slightly tilted book and watch:

  • Roll — the sphere rolls in any direction, the cylinder rolls on its side, and the cone rolls in a curve because one end is wider.
  • Slide — the cube and cuboid slide on their flat faces but will not roll, thanks to those corners.
  • Stack — the cube and cuboid stack neatly, a cylinder stacks if you rest it on its flat end, and a sphere refuses to stack at all.

The honest surprise here is the cylinder: it both rolls and stacks, depending on which way you set it down. Stand a tin on its end and it stacks like a box; lay it on its side and it rolls away. Let a child discover that themselves rather than telling them — the ‘oh!’ moment is the learning.

Spotting 3D shapes at home

Turn the kitchen into a shape hunt. A packet of biscuits, a football, a birthday cap, a water bottle, a rolling pin — each one is a solid from the table above. Ask your child to name the shape and then count its faces by touching each surface. Ten minutes of this beats any amount of diagram-copying, and it is free.

One trap to avoid: a book or a mobile phone is a cuboid, not a ‘rectangle’. A rectangle is flat, a cuboid is solid. Keeping 2D and 3D words separate now saves a lot of confusion in Grade 3.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly these solids — faces, edges, vertices, and which shapes roll or stack. Let your child answer, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key you can print again and again.

quiz.title: Grade 2 3D Shapes Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on cubes, cuboids, spheres, cones and cylinders - their faces, edges, vertices and whether they roll or stack. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 solid shapes and their properties

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 flat square faces, like the six sides of a dice.

questions.q: How many vertices (corners) does a cuboid have?
questions.explanation: A cuboid, like a matchbox, has 8 corners where its edges meet.

questions.q: Which solid has no edges and no vertices?
questions.explanation: A sphere is one smooth curved surface - like a ball - with no edges and no corners.

questions.q: How many edges does a cylinder have?
questions.explanation: A cylinder, like a tin, has 2 edges - the circles where its curved surface meets each flat end.

questions.q: Which everyday object is a cone?
questions.explanation: An ice-cream cone has one flat circle at the bottom and one point on top - that is a cone.
A sphere is round all over, so it rolls in every direction. Cubes and cuboids only slide.

questions.q: How many vertices does a cone have?
questions.explanation: A cone has exactly 1 vertex - the single point at the top.

questions.q: Which solid can both roll and stack, depending on how you place it?
questions.explanation: Stand a cylinder on its flat end and it stacks; lay it on its side and it rolls.

faq.q: What is the difference between a face, an edge and a vertex?
faq.a: A face is a flat or curved surface you could paint. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner point where edges meet — the plural is vertices.

faq.q: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have?
faq.a: A cube has 6 flat square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A cuboid, such as a matchbox, has exactly the same numbers — only the face sizes differ.

faq.q: Why does a sphere have no edges or vertices?
faq.a: A sphere is a single smooth curved surface with nothing flat to meet along a line and no corner points. A ball or an orange shows this — roll it and there is no edge to feel.

faq.q: Which 3D shapes roll and which stack?
faq.a: Spheres, cones and cylinders roll because of their curved surfaces. Cubes and cuboids stack neatly on their flat faces. A cylinder is special: it stacks on its flat end and rolls on its side.
